title: The First Modern Railway
summary: In 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first railway where steam trains carried people between two big cities on a timetable. Builders even floated the track across a squishy bog! Soon everyone in Britain wanted railways, and a fight broke out over how wide the tracks should be.

sections.heading: Carving a Path Between Two Cities
paragraphs: The Stockton and Darlington had been a coal railway that also carried some passengers. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway was meant to be something much bolder: a railway built from the start to carry both people and goods, quickly and regularly, between two big, busy cities. To do that, George Stephenson wanted a line that was as flat and straight as possible, because even the best locomotives of the time struggled on hills. That meant the land itself had to be reshaped.

Getting permission was a battle in its own right. Canal owners, stagecoach companies and powerful landowners, including aristocrats who did not want noisy engines crossing their estates, fought the plan in Parliament. The railway's first attempt to win an Act of Parliament failed in 1825, partly because Stephenson's early survey contained mistakes that opposing lawyers pounced on. The company had the route surveyed again more carefully, steering it away from some of the hostile estates, and the Act finally passed in 1826. Work could begin.

At the Liverpool end, the railway needed to reach the docks, which lay far below the higher ground east of the town. So the engineers dug the Wapping Tunnel, about 2,250 yards (around 2 kilometres) long, running under the streets of Liverpool from Edge Hill down to the docks. It is thought to be the first tunnel ever bored beneath a city. Its walls were whitewashed and lit by gas lamps so that early visitors could walk through and admire it. Interestingly, the locomotives did not work the steep tunnels at first. Wagons ran down by gravity and were hauled back up by ropes from stationary engines at Edge Hill, so the rival technology from Rainhill still had a small job to do after all.

Just east of Edge Hill came the Olive Mount cutting. Rather than climb over a ridge of solid sandstone, the line went straight through it, in a man-made canyon about 2 miles (3 kilometres) long and up to about 70 feet (21 metres) deep. It was dug almost entirely by hand, with picks, shovels, gunpowder for blasting, and horses and carts to haul the rock away. The men who did this heavy work were called navvies, short for 'navigators', a name first given to the labourers who dug Britain's canals. Much of the stone they removed was reused to build bridges and walls along the line.

Further east, the railway had to cross the valley of the Sankey Brook, which also carried a canal. The canal company insisted that its boats, flat-bottomed sailing barges called Mersey flats, must still be able to pass underneath with their masts up. So Stephenson designed the Sankey Viaduct: nine great arches of brick and sandstone, each spanning 50 feet (15 metres), carrying the track about 60 to 70 feet (around 20 metres) above the valley. It cost about 45,000 pounds, a huge sum. It is often called the world's earliest major railway viaduct, it is protected today as a Grade I listed structure, and trains still rumble across it, nearly two centuries later.

Altogether the line needed 64 bridges and viaducts, almost all of brick or stone. In Manchester, the line crossed Water Street on an early cast-iron bridge, and ended at a modest station on Liverpool Road. That building still stands. It is thought to be the oldest surviving railway terminus in the world, and today it is part of the Science and Industry Museum.

sections.heading: Floating Across Chat Moss
paragraphs: The hardest problem of all lay only a few miles west of Manchester. It was a vast, wobbly peat bog called Chat Moss, covering about 10 square miles (27 square kilometres). Its peat, made of dead plants soaked in water, was in places around 24 to 30 feet deep. In wet weather it was so soft that a person could sink into it, and it was said that a stick pushed into it could disappear completely. Some engineers had told Parliament that building a railway across it was impossible.

Stephenson's first idea was simple: pour in enough earth and rubble to reach the solid ground underneath and build an embankment on top. At one especially bad spot, known as Blackpool Hole, gangs of workers tipped load after load of spoil into the bog for weeks on end, and it simply vanished, sinking or squeezing out sideways into the soft peat. The bog seemed to swallow everything.

So Stephenson changed his approach, with advice from Robert Stannard, a man with long experience of working on marshland. Instead of trying to reach the bottom, they decided to float the railway on top, rather like a raft. Workers laid down great mats, or hurdles, made of heather and brushwood (bundles of branches) bound together. On top of these they spread layers of earth, rubble and cinders, and then laid the track on wooden sleepers in a herringbone pattern, which spread the weight of a train over a wide area. Ditches were dug along both sides to drain water away, and old tar barrels were used to line the drains. Where the bog was deepest, the line rested on this floating mat, which bent slightly as a train passed but did not sink.

It took time, patience and enormous amounts of material, but it worked. The crossing, about 4 and three-quarter miles (7.6 kilometres) long, was finished by the end of 1829. On 28 December that year, Rocket crossed it pulling a carriage of about 40 passengers, taking around 17 minutes. Amazingly, the floating foundation, strengthened over the years, still supports the main line between Liverpool and Manchester today, carrying trains far heavier than anything Stephenson could have imagined.

sections.heading: A Grand Opening, 15 September 1830
paragraphs: Picture Liverpool on the morning of Wednesday 15 September 1830. Huge crowds pack the streets near the Edge Hill area, where the trains will start. Flags flutter, bands play, cannon are fired, and the people who have paid for tickets settle into their carriages in their finest clothes. Eight locomotives built by Robert Stephenson and Company stand ready, among them Northumbrian, Phoenix, North Star, Rocket, Dart, Comet, Arrow and Meteor, each pulling a train of carriages. It is the grandest railway event the world has ever seen.

The guest of honour was the Duke of Wellington, the Prime Minister and the hero who had defeated Napoleon at Waterloo 15 years earlier. He rode in a special, richly decorated carriage, pulled by the newest and best engine, Northumbrian, with George Stephenson himself at the controls. The Duke's train ran on one of the two tracks, the southern line. The other seven trains followed on the northern track, so that they could run alongside and pass the Duke's train, letting their passengers see and cheer him.

Because this was the first railway with two tracks all the way, trains could travel in both directions at once, or pass each other, without waiting. That seems normal today, but it was new in 1830, and it shaped the day in ways nobody planned.

The trains set off eastwards towards Manchester, cheered by crowds lining the cuttings and fields. Passengers were thrilled by the speed and by the views from the Sankey Viaduct. Some had already tasted this new sensation. Before the line opened, the famous young actress Fanny Kemble had been given a ride on the footplate by George Stephenson during a test run. In a letter she compared the engine to a living animal, a snorting little horse, and wrote warmly of Stephenson himself. Many of the guests on opening day felt the same mixture of excitement and wonder.
Halfway along the line, at a place called Parkside, near Newton, the trains stopped so the engines could take on water. That short stop would become one of the most famous moments in railway history.

sections.heading: Tragedy at Parkside
paragraphs: Among the guests in the Duke of Wellington's train was William Huskisson, the Member of Parliament for Liverpool. He was about 60 years old, an important politician who had served as President of the Board of Trade and had championed freer trade, which mattered greatly to a port city like Liverpool. He had been a strong supporter of the railway. He was not in good health, and a royal doctor had even advised him to cancel his engagements, but he came anyway.

Huskisson and Wellington had quarrelled two years earlier, when Huskisson resigned from Wellington's government. Many people hoped the opening day might be a chance to make peace. While Northumbrian was taking on water at Parkside, a number of passengers ignored instructions to stay in their seats and climbed down onto the track to stretch their legs. Huskisson walked over to the Duke's carriage, and the Duke reached out to shake his hand.

At that moment, Rocket, driven by the young engineer Joseph Locke, came steaming along the other track. People shouted warnings. There was very little space between the two lines, and Huskisson, who was not quick on his feet, tried to climb into the Duke's carriage. But its door had not been fastened, and it swung open, leaving him hanging in Rocket's path. He fell onto the rails, and Rocket ran over his leg, injuring it terribly. Locke had tried to stop, but early locomotives had no proper brakes on their wheels; reversing the engine took several seconds to have any effect.

George Stephenson acted fast. He uncoupled Northumbrian from the Duke's train, attached a single carriage, and Huskisson was laid on a door taken from a nearby building and lifted aboard. Stephenson then drove as fast as he dared to the town of Eccles, more than 10 miles further along the line towards Manchester, to find doctors. Some accounts say Northumbrian reached around 35 miles per hour on this desperate run, faster than people had ever travelled, though such early speed figures are hard to check. Sadly, the doctors could do little. Huskisson was carried to the vicarage at Eccles, where he was cared for by the vicar's wife and joined by his wife, Emily. He was able to make his will, and he died at about 9 o'clock that evening.

Huskisson was not the first person ever killed by a railway. Workers and bystanders had already been hurt and killed on earlier lines. But his death, in front of the Prime Minister and hundreds of the most important people in the country, was one of the first railway passenger deaths reported far and wide. Newspapers everywhere carried the story. It was a shocking lesson that these powerful new machines, so quiet compared to their speed, needed new rules: stay inside the train, and never stand on the track.

The rest of the day was gloomy. The Duke of Wellington wanted to turn back, but the organisers persuaded him to go on to Manchester, where huge crowds were waiting. Wellington was very unpopular in parts of Manchester, where many working people were angry about poverty and the lack of votes for ordinary people. Some of the crowd booed and threw things at his carriage. The Duke stayed in his seat and soon headed back towards Liverpool. Some of the trains did not get home until late at night, in the rain.

sections.heading: Why It Was the First Modern Railway
paragraphs: Despite that sad start, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened to the public the very next day and quickly proved its worth. Historians often call it the first truly modern railway, because it brought together, for the first time, almost all the features we expect a railway to have.

It joined two big cities, rather than a mine and a river. It had double track the whole way, a little over 30 miles (about 50 kilometres) from Liverpool to Manchester, so trains could run in both directions at once. Every train on the main line was pulled by a steam locomotive; there were no horse-drawn coaches mixed in, as there had been on the Stockton and Darlington. It was run by the company itself, which owned the engines and carriages, employed the drivers, and ran trains to a published timetable, so passengers knew when to turn up. Passengers bought tickets for their journey, with different classes of carriage at different prices. And it carried both people and goods: passengers from the start, and freight from December 1830, once the more powerful locomotive Planet had arrived.

The journey between the two cities took about two hours. That might not sound fast to us, but the railway was quicker, smoother and more reliable than the stagecoaches that bumped along the roads, and much faster than the canal barges. Early passenger trains averaged around 16 miles per hour and goods trains about 8.

Then came the biggest surprise. The railway's founders had expected to make most of their money from cotton and other goods. Instead, people flocked to ride the trains. Within a few weeks of opening, the Manchester station was handling around 800 passengers a day, and on some days as many as 2,500 travellers. Within a short time, most of the stagecoach services between Liverpool and Manchester simply closed down; there was no point competing. The railway also began carrying mail, and ran special excursion trains for people simply wanting a day out.

The canal companies fought back by cutting their prices, and a price war followed, which was good news for merchants. Even so, the railway made healthy profits. Over its 15 years as an independent company, shareholders received an average dividend, or yearly payout, of about 9.5 percent of their investment. Bankers and businesspeople all over Britain took notice. If a railway could do this well between Liverpool and Manchester, why not between every pair of big towns in the country?

Engineers took notice too. Visitors came from America, France, Germany and beyond to study the line. Railways soon followed linking London with Birmingham, Birmingham with Liverpool and Manchester, and many more. By the late 1830s, Britain was building a network.

sections.heading: Railway Mania
paragraphs: By the mid-1840s, railway fever had gripped Britain. The economy was recovering after hard times, interest rates were low, and people with savings were looking for something exciting to invest in. Railways seemed like the perfect choice: they were new, they were clearly useful, and the early lines like the Liverpool and Manchester had paid well. Newspapers filled up with advertisements for new railway companies, each promising to build a line somewhere and pay rich rewards. This frenzy is known as Railway Mania.

To build a railway in Britain, a company needed its own Act of Parliament, giving it the right to buy land along its route. In 1846 alone, at the peak of the mania, Parliament passed 263 Acts setting up new railway companies, with plans for about 9,500 miles (15,300 kilometres) of track. Many Members of Parliament were themselves investors in railways, so there was little appetite to slow things down. Some schemes were sensible. Others were wildly unrealistic, proposing lines between small villages, or competing lines that duplicated each other almost side by side.

Like many booms, it ended in a bust. In late 1845 the Bank of England raised interest rates, borrowing money became more expensive, and investors began to panic. Share prices tumbled. Thousands of people, from wealthy gentlemen to shopkeepers and widows who had put in their savings, lost money, sometimes everything. About a third of the railways that had been authorised were never built at all. Bigger, stronger companies bought up struggling ones cheaply.

Yet the mania left something lasting behind. About 6,220 miles (10,000 kilometres) of railway were eventually built from the schemes approved between 1844 and 1846. That is more than half the length of Britain's whole railway network today. The country ended up with railways reaching almost every town, even if many investors paid dearly for them. Historians still compare Railway Mania with later investment bubbles, such as the dot-com boom of the late 1990s, when people rushed to invest in new internet companies.

Parliament did try to set some rules. A law of 1844, pushed through by William Gladstone, who was then in charge of the Board of Trade, required every railway company to run at least one cheap train a day each way along its lines, in covered carriages, stopping at every station, for a fare of no more than one penny a mile. These 'parliamentary trains' meant that even poorer people could afford to travel by rail.

sections.heading: The Railway King
paragraphs: The most famous figure of Railway Mania was George Hudson. Born in 1800 to a farming family in Yorkshire, he became a draper, a cloth merchant, in the city of York. After he came into a large inheritance, he began investing in railways, and he turned out to be a brilliant and ruthless dealmaker.

Hudson saw that many small railway companies would be stronger joined together. He chaired the York and North Midland Railway, helped create the Midland Railway in 1844 by merging three companies, and went on to control a large share of the lines in the north and middle of England. He turned York into one of Britain's great railway junctions, served several times as Lord Mayor of York, and became a Member of Parliament for Sunderland. In 1844 the writer Sydney Smith gave him the nickname that stuck: 'the Railway King'.

But Hudson's empire had a rotten secret. To keep shareholders happy and share prices high, he paid out generous dividends. Some of that money did not come from profits at all, but from new capital, the money investors had just put in to build more railways. In effect, he was paying old investors with new investors' money, and keeping misleading accounts to hide it. When the mania collapsed, investors started asking hard questions. Inquiries in 1849 exposed his methods. Hudson lost his positions, was declared bankrupt, and spent years living abroad to avoid being imprisoned for debt. He returned to England only after imprisonment for debt was abolished in 1870, and died in London in 1871.

Hudson's story shows both sides of the railway boom. He really did help build a more connected network, and some of his mergers made good sense. But his dishonesty hurt many ordinary people, and it helped persuade later governments that big companies needed proper accounts and closer checks.

sections.heading: Brunel and the Battle of the Gauges
paragraphs: While northern railways copied Stephenson's 4 feet 8 and a half inch gauge, one brilliant engineer in the west of England decided to do things differently. Isambard Kingdom Brunel was only in his late twenties when he became engineer of the Great Western Railway, planned to run from London to Bristol. Brunel thought big. He believed a much wider track would let trains run faster and more smoothly, with bigger carriages, larger wagons and room for large wheels and boilers. Having watched carriages swaying on the Stockton and Darlington, he chose a broad gauge of 7 feet and a quarter of an inch (about 2,140 millimetres), more than half as wide again as Stephenson's.

The Great Western's first section, from Paddington in London to Maidenhead, opened to the public on 4 June 1838, and the whole line to Bristol was ready by 30 June 1841. It was a superb railway, laid out with very gentle slopes and curves, and its broad-gauge trains were among the fastest in the world. Many travellers agreed they were smoother and more comfortable too.

The trouble came where the two systems met. At Gloucester, broad-gauge trains from the Great Western met standard-gauge trains from the Midlands. Passengers had to get off with their luggage and change trains, and every sack, crate and parcel had to be unloaded by hand from one wagon and loaded into another, which could take hours. Newspapers and cartoonists mocked the chaos on the platforms. This messy meeting point was called a 'break of gauge', and as both networks grew, the arguments between their supporters became known as the Gauge War.

In 1845 the government set up a Royal Commission to decide what to do. Both sides staged speed trials. A broad-gauge engine called Ixion averaged about 53 miles per hour between Paddington and Didcot, carrying heavier loads than its rival, while a standard-gauge engine trying to match it on the line between Darlington and York came off the rails. The broad gauge clearly performed better, but by then there were far more miles of standard-gauge track. Changing all of those would cost a fortune. The commission decided that having one gauge mattered more than having the best one.

So in 1846 Parliament passed the Gauge Act, which said that new railways for passengers in Great Britain must be built to 4 feet 8 and a half inches, unless they were extensions of the existing broad-gauge network. (Ireland, a separate system, settled on its own gauge of 5 feet 3 inches.) The Great Western kept its broad gauge for decades and added a third rail to many lines, creating 'mixed gauge' track that both kinds of trains could use. But step by step it gave in. Brunel died in 1859, and conversion began in the 1860s. Finally, in a huge operation in May 1892, thousands of workers converted the last broad-gauge main line, through Devon to Penzance in Cornwall, in about two days. By 21 May 1892 the broad gauge was gone, and its engines were towed away to Swindon to be scrapped.

In just over 60 years, from Rainhill to the end of the Gauge War, the railway had gone from an experiment to a nationwide system that changed how Britain lived and worked. But what really happens inside one of these puffing machines? In the next part, it is time to climb up onto the footplate, the platform where the driver and fireman stand, and see exactly how a steam locomotive works.

deepDive: Why do historians call the Liverpool and Manchester Railway the first modern railway, when the Stockton and Darlington opened five years earlier? The answer is the combination of features: double track throughout, steam traction only on the main line, a company that operated its own trains rather than charging tolls to independent carriers, scheduled services, ticketing, and both passengers and freight. Its economics surprised everyone. The promoters had planned around cotton and goods, but passenger traffic became a major source of income, and stagecoach services between the two cities collapsed. The line averaged a dividend of about 9.5 percent over 15 years, a figure that helped trigger later investment waves. There are a few points of debate and uncertainty. Figures for the line's length vary from about 30 to 35 miles depending on which termini and branches are counted; the main route from Liverpool to Manchester was a little over 30 miles. Opening-day speeds are also uncertain: the often-quoted figure of about 35 mph for Northumbrian's emergency run to Eccles comes from witnesses without precise timing. Huskisson's death is sometimes called the first railway fatality, but that is not true; it was among the first widely reported passenger deaths. Railway Mania is studied by economists as a classic speculative bubble. In 1846, 263 Acts authorised about 9,500 miles of new line, yet about a third was never built, while some 6,220 miles were eventually completed from the 1844 to 1846 approvals. Economists debate whether the bubble was wasteful or whether, like the late-1990s fibre-optic boom, it left behind valuable infrastructure that society would not otherwise have funded. The Gauge War raises a classic question in technology: the 'better' standard does not always win. Brunel's broad gauge offered stability and space, but the network effect of the larger standard-gauge system, and the cost of converting it, decided the outcome. Similar battles happened later with videotape formats, plugs and charging connectors.
funFact: The track across the Chat Moss bog, floated on mats of heather and brushwood in 1829, still carries trains between Liverpool and Manchester today.
